english_translation: Our trip to the mountains was truly wonderful; although we encountered heavy rain along the way, we all managed to arrive safely.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('takasangana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'takasangana' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('rwedu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'rwedu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

cultural_notes.title: Scenic Excursions to Zimbabwe's Mountain Ranges ('Kuenda kuMakomo')
cultural_notes.content: Trips to Zimbabwe's mountain regions—such as Mt Nyangani (the country's highest peak), the Vumba Mountains, or Chimanimani—often feature misty mountain showers ('mvura yakawanda') alongside breathtaking views.

active_exercises.prompt: In a Zimbabwean city, if a driver says 'Mota dzakamira parobhoti dzichimirira mwenje wegirinhi', where are the cars stopped?
options: At a rural bus stop waiting for passengers
Inside a garage having their tyres repaired
At the traffic light waiting for the green light
Beside a river bridge that is under construction
active_exercises.correct_answer: At the traffic light waiting for the green light
active_exercises.explanation: 'Robhoti' (plural 'marobhotsi') is the standard Shona word for a traffic light, and 'mwenje wegirinhi' is the green light.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this sentence about travelling: 'Mangwana ______ bhazi rinoenda kuMasvingo.' (Tomorrow we will board the bus going to Masvingo.)
Complete this new sentence in the past tense: 'Nezuro amai ______ sadza nenyama.' (Yesterday Mother cooked sadza and meat.)
active_exercises.explanation: 'Amai' takes the respectful plural past prefix 'vaka-' + '-bika' (cook) -> 'vakabika' ('cooked').
